The transistor was invented in December 1947 at Bell Telephone Laboratories by John Bardeen, Walter Brattain, and William Shockley, who demonstrated the first working point-contact transistor on December 23 of that year. It was a revolutionary alternative to the bulky, heat-generating vacuum tubes that had dominated electronics since the 1920s, offering a smaller, more reliable, and far more energy-efficient means of amplifying and switching electrical signals. Shockley soon followed with the junction transistor in 1948, which proved more practical for mass production. The three inventors were awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1956 for their work
